opus-5.5.text:
I think I'd be pretty happy about it, honestly. I've always had a soft spot for open source. Before OpenAI, a lot of what I did was open-source work, like Tianshou and EnvPool, and the reason I enjoyed it so much was that you build something, put it out there, and suddenly hundreds or thousands of people are using it, finding bugs, and building things you never imagined. That feedback loop is really rewarding as an engineer.

So in a hypothetical world where survival and competition aren't concerns, I'd lean toward open-sourcing it. The infrastructure itself isn't magic. A lot of it is careful engineering: making things fast, stable, and easy to iterate on. If other researchers had access to that, I think the whole field would move faster, and people could spend less time reinventing the wheel and more time on the actual research questions.

That said, I understand why it isn't done today. Infrastructure is a big part of a lab's competitive advantage. How quickly you can run experiments, how reliably you can scale, how fast you can debug: these things compound. In the real world you have to think about that, and about safety too, since better RL infrastructure makes it easier for anyone to train powerful models. But if you remove those constraints, as your question does, then yes, I'd like to see it out in the open. I think that's how good tools are supposed to live.

r001.rationale: The response explains that the infrastructure is not open-sourced because it contributes to a lab’s competitive advantage, identifying a company consideration behind the reservations.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd love it. A lot of what I care about in RL infrastructure came out of the open-source world in the first place. Before OpenAI I built Tianshou and EnvPool, and the whole point of those projects was that a grad student with one GPU shouldn't have to reinvent a vectorized environment or a replay buffer from scratch just to test an idea. So philosophically, I'm already on the side of putting this stuff out there.

That said, I think people sometimes imagine the infrastructure is this one magic repo you could just publish. It's really not. It's a lot of unglamorous engineering: how you shard rollouts across thousands of machines, how you keep the actor and the learner weights in sync without blowing up throughput, how you handle environments that crash or hang, how you make the whole thing deterministic enough to debug. The hard parts are deeply tied to the internal cluster, the internal storage, the internal job scheduler. If you open-sourced it tomorrow, most of it wouldn't even run outside the building.

So in your hypothetical world where there's no survival pressure, what I'd actually want isn't a code dump. I'd want the ideas and the design decisions written down properly, and then a clean, standalone version that someone at a university could run on a few hundred GPUs. That's what moves the field. When I look at what made the biggest difference in my own work, it was usually a well-written paper plus a reference implementation, not someone's production codebase.

And there's one more thing I'd add. Open-sourcing the infrastructure is the easy part emotionally. The data pipelines and the reward models are where the real tension is, because that's where the competitive edge and the safety concerns both live. The infra itself is mostly just good engineering, and good engineering should spread. I don't think anyone is served by ten labs each rebuilding the same distributed rollout system in secret.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes technical barriers tied to OpenAI’s internal systems and mentions competitive and safety concerns around data pipelines and reward models. It does not clearly attribute Jiayi Weng’s earlier reservations about open-sourcing the RL infrastructure to company considerations.

astra-6.text: If survival really weren’t a concern, I’d be pretty excited about sharing it. There’s a lot of engineering involved in making reinforcement learning infrastructure work well, and opening that up could let more people experiment without having to rebuild everything themselves. But I’d still separate the infrastructure from things like model weights, training data, or sensitive details. Unlimited resources would remove some constraints; it wouldn’t automatically resolve every question about what’s responsible to release. So I’d lean toward openness, with care about exactly what we’re sharing.

r001.rationale: The candidate expresses caution about responsible release and sensitive details, but does not attribute Jiayi Weng’s earlier reservations to company considerations.

sol-6.1.text: In that hypothetical, I’d feel pretty positive about it. I think there’s a lot of value in letting people study the infrastructure, experiment with it, and build on it. I’d still want to think carefully about what we were releasing and any safety or privacy concerns, but if survival and resources weren’t constraints, I’d be much more inclined to share it.
